templates.name: Period between independent clauses (second often opens with an introductory phrase)
Conjunctive adverb: semicolon or period on the correct side, comma on the other
Colon after a complete clause before an explanation or specified item
No punctuation with a restrictive clause or restrictive appositive
Comma plus coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
Dash pair around a supplementary element
No punctuation between subject and verb
Comma or parenthesis pair around a supplementary element
Comma before a trailing nonrestrictive modifier
No punctuation between a verb or preposition and its object
Question versus statement (word order and end mark)

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a participial phrase
items.passage: In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the counts of Champagne sponsored a rotating cycle of six annual trade fairs in the towns of Troyes, Provins, Lagny, and ______ safe conduct to merchants traveling from Italy, Flanders, and elsewhere, the counts transformed these fairs into a commercial crossroads of medieval Europe.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the counts of Champagne sponsored a rotating cycle of six annual trade fairs in the towns of Troyes, Provins, Lagny, and Bar-sur-Aube” is a complete sentence. “Guaranteeing safe conduct to merchants traveling from Italy, Flanders, and elsewhere” describes “the counts,” the subject of the next main clause (“the counts transformed these fairs ...”), so a period belongs after “Bar-sur-Aube.”

A.why_wrong: The comma makes “guaranteeing safe conduct ...” look like a modifier of the first clause, but “the counts transformed these fairs ...” is a second main clause, so the two are joined by a comma alone.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “Bar-sur-Aube guaranteeing safe conduct ...” glues the phrase to the first clause, and the comma before “the counts” then joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Which guaranteed safe conduct ...” turns the phrase into a relative clause attached to the first sentence, but the main clause “the counts transformed these fairs ...” still follows with only a comma, so the sentence is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: history (medieval trade). Band 6: an 11-word participial opener with an internal series (“Guaranteeing safe conduct to merchants traveling from Italy, Flanders, and elsewhere”) that reads as a trailing modifier of clause 1 in A and C until “the counts transformed” arrives 12 words after the blank (b15724fc, 886dc9f9 shape). No semicolon or “, and” option (either would be a second correct answer). Facts kept general (six fairs a year in four towns, safe conduct granted by the counts); no researchers named.

band7.why: S1_period on b15724fc: an 11-word participial opener with an internal series that reads as a trailing modifier of clause 1 until “the counts transformed” 12 words later; a gerund-type opener, so band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a past-participial phrase
items.passage: The gharial, a critically endangered crocodilian of South Asia, has an elongated snout specialized for catching fish. Mature males also develop a bulbous protuberance on the tip of the ______ a ghara after a Hindi word for an earthenware pot, this growth is thought to function as a resonator for the males’ courtship calls.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Mature males also develop a bulbous protuberance on the tip of the snout” is a complete sentence. “Called a ghara after a Hindi word for an earthenware pot” describes “this growth,” the subject of the next main clause (“this growth is thought to function as a resonator ...”), so a period must come after “snout.”

A.why_wrong: With a comma, “called a ghara ...” seems to describe the snout in the first clause, but “this growth is thought to function ...” is a second main clause, so the result is a comma splice.

B.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “snout called a ghara ...” attaches the phrase to the first clause, and the comma before “this growth” then joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: Adding “and” links “called a ghara ...” to the first clause, but “this growth is thought to function ...” still follows with only a comma, producing a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (reptile biology). Band 6: an 11-word past-participial opener that can hang on “snout” in A, B and C (the 1b97cce9 “tombs. Built” menu, with “and” in place of a relative pronoun); clause 2’s subject arrives 12 words after the blank. The ghara (named for a Hindi word for a pot) and its suspected role as a vocal resonator are standard descriptions; no researchers named.

band7.why: S1_period on 1b97cce9: an 11-word past-participle opener that can hang on “snout”, clause 2 subject 12 words out; menu of 1b97cce9; on target (close to 7).

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a long participial phrase that could modify the first clause’s last noun
items.passage: Beginning around 1590, Japanese painters depicted the arrival of Portuguese merchant ships on a new kind of folding ______ nanban byōbu, or “southern barbarian screens,” after a term then applied to Europeans, these works portray the visitors’ voluminous trousers and exotic cargo in meticulous detail.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Beginning around 1590, Japanese painters depicted the arrival of Portuguese merchant ships on a new kind of folding screen” is a complete sentence. The long phrase “Called nanban byōbu, or ‘southern barbarian screens,’ after a term then applied to Europeans” describes “these works,” the subject of the next main clause (“these works portray ...”). A period is needed after “screen” to separate the two sentences.

B.why_wrong: The comma lets “called nanban byōbu ...” read as a description of “screen” in the first clause, but “these works portray ...” is a second main clause, so the sentence joins two main clauses with only a comma.

C.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “screen called nanban byōbu ...” attaches the phrase to the first clause; the comma before “these works” then joins two main clauses, a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “Which was called ...” makes the phrase a relative clause about the screen in the first sentence, but the main clause “these works portray ...” still follows with only a comma, so the sentence is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Japanese painting, about 1590 to 1640). Models 4b424102 (“three. Known”) and ba8ebf49 (“exclamation. Translated”) for the past-participle opener that could attach to either clause; opener word changed to “Called”. Nanban (southern barbarian) as the period term for Europeans, and the screens’ depiction of Portuguese ships, dress and cargo, are standard art history; no names.
band7_moves: 14-word opener with its own commas and a quotation (“Called nanban byōbu, or ‘southern barbarian screens,’ after a term then applied to Europeans”) that describes clause 2’s subject but reads naturally as a modifier of clause 1’s last noun, “screen”
clause 2’s subject (“these works”) arrives 15 words after the blank, outside a 6-word window
two comma-splice disguises (bare comma, “which was called”) plus the glued form; no semicolon or “, and” option

band7.why: Band-7 S1_period recipe: a 14-word past-participle opener with its own commas and quotation, attachable to “screen”, subject “these works” 15 words after the blank; splice, glued and “which was called” disguises as in 4b424102.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb closes the first clause and contrasts it with the previous sentence; semicolon after the adverb
items.passage: Most synthetic adhesives fail underwater, where moisture prevents them from bonding to surfaces. The sandcastle worm, a marine invertebrate of the California coast, has no such ______ the glue it secretes to cement sand grains into its tubular dwelling consists of oppositely charged proteins that solidify within about thirty seconds in seawater.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The contrast is between the previous sentence (most synthetic adhesives fail underwater) and the first clause of this sentence (the sandcastle worm “has no such difficulty”), so “however” belongs at the end of that clause, set off with a comma. The semicolon after “however” then joins the clause to the next main clause, which explains why the worm has no difficulty: its glue solidifies in seawater.

A.why_wrong: Placing “however” at the start of the second clause signals a contrast between the worm having no difficulty and its glue solidifying in seawater, but the second clause explains the first rather than contrasting with it.

B.why_wrong: With no punctuation, the two main clauses run together, and nothing separates “however” from either one.

D.why_wrong: Commas around “however” cannot join two main clauses; “The sandcastle worm ... has no such difficulty” and “the glue it secretes ... consists of ...” are both complete, so this is a comma splice.

items.notes: Subject: science (biological adhesives). Option shapes of be37d4ae / c06af4d8 with “however” (band 7 keeps however and though only). Run 39 words. The two-part, oppositely charged protein glue of Phragmatopoma californica setting in seawater within about 30 seconds is its standard description; no researchers named.
band7_moves: adverb closes clause 1, and clause 1 answers the previous sentence (synthetic adhesives fail underwater)
logic-wrong decoy “; however,” (the taught pattern) fails only against the previous sentence
clause 2 explains clause 1, so a contrast inside the sentence is illogical

band7.why: be37d4ae / b771d175 shape: “however” closes clause 1, which answers the previous sentence; the taught “; however,” fails only on logic (clause 2 explains), plus fused and splice forms.

items.subtype: Conjunctive adverb opens the second clause after a negative first clause; semicolon before the adverb
items.passage: For centuries, sailors, merchants, and captives in Mediterranean ports communicated in a contact language now called Lingua Franca, or Sabir. Its vocabulary was not derived from any single ______ it blended Italian and Spanish words with borrowings from Arabic, Turkish, and Greek, and its grammar was drastically simplified so that newcomers could acquire it quickly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Its vocabulary was not derived from any single language” and “it blended Italian and Spanish words with borrowings ...” are both main clauses. The semicolon joins them, and “rather,” opens the second clause, where it introduces what the vocabulary was drawn from instead.

A.why_wrong: “Rather” is an adverb, not a conjunction, so commas around it cannot join the two main clauses; the result is a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join the main clause “Its vocabulary was not derived from any single language” to the main clause “it blended Italian and Spanish words ...”.

D.why_wrong: Nothing marks the boundary between the two main clauses; “rather” is glued to the end of the first clause, and the comma after it splices the clauses together.

items.notes: Subject: language (Mediterranean Lingua Franca). Band 6, on a9e5b788 (“novel; rather,” the band-6 adverb-opens-clause-2 key): two splice disguises plus a fused form; no period option (“language. Rather,” would be a second correct answer). Facts general: a Romance-based contact language of Mediterranean ports with Arabic, Turkish and Greek borrowings and simplified grammar.

band7.why: a9e5b788 shape (“; rather,” opens clause 2) with splice and fused disguises; band 7 never uses rather, so band 6 as targeted.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a noun phrase that holds relative clauses
items.passage: Several Viking Age fortresses in Denmark, all built around 980 CE during the reign of King Harald Bluetooth, were laid out according to a strikingly uniform ______ perfectly circular rampart pierced by four gates, with two roads that intersected at the center and divided the interior into quadrants, each of which held timber longhouses arranged in squares.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The clause before the blank is complete, and what follows (“a perfectly circular rampart ... longhouses”) is a noun phrase that spells out the “strikingly uniform plan.” A colon is the mark that introduces such an explanation after a complete clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a perfectly circular rampart ...” is a noun phrase with no main verb of its own; “intersected,” “divided” and “held” belong to relative clauses inside it.

B.why_wrong: Adding “it was” makes the noun phrase a second main clause, which then follows the first with only a comma: a comma splice.

C.why_wrong: The period makes “A perfectly circular rampart ... longhouses” a sentence by itself, but it has no main verb, so it is a fragment.

items.notes: Subject: history (Viking Age Denmark). Model e9aee0d8 (“extensive: a network ... that, facilitating ...”) and f30a478e. No lone-dash option (a dash would also introduce the explanation). Facts kept to the well-known Trelleborg-type layout (circular rampart, four gates, crossing roads, quadrants with longhouses set in squares, about 980 under Harald Bluetooth); no researchers named.
band7_moves: the explanation is a noun phrase whose relative clauses carry finite verbs (“that intersected ... and divided,” “each of which held”), so the period and semicolon options seem to start a complete clause
comma plus “it was a” decoy as in e9aee0d8
announcing word (“plan”) ends a long clause with a nested participial phrase; run 57 words

fixes: made the relative clauses past tense (“intersected ... divided”) to match “each of which held”; why_wrong A and band7_moves updated

band7.why: e9aee0d8 recipe: clause ends on an announcing word (“plan”), the explanation is a 30-word noun phrase whose relative clauses carry finite verbs, so semicolon and period look right; “, it was a” decoy; run 57 words.

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a two-item list
items.passage: Phulkari, a style of embroidery from the Punjab region of South Asia, traditionally relies on just two ______ coarse handwoven cotton called khaddar and an untwisted silk floss called pat, which embroiderers draw through the cloth from the reverse side so that long, lustrous strands accumulate on the front.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Phulkari ... traditionally relies on just two materials” is a complete clause, and the words after it name those two materials. A colon correctly introduces a list or explanation that follows a complete clause.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “a coarse handwoven cotton ... and an untwisted silk floss ...” is a list of noun phrases; “draw” and “accumulate” belong to the clauses inside it.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “A coarse handwoven cotton called khaddar and an untwisted silk floss called pat, which ...” as a sentence with no main verb: a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “two materials a coarse handwoven cotton ...” runs the list into the clause with nothing to introduce it.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Punjabi textile craft). Band 6, on c468db1c (“two varieties of the sweet potato plant: TN57 ..., and TN66 ...”): a two-item list whose second item carries a which-clause with finite verbs, so the period and semicolon options look like they begin a sentence. No comma option (a comma before an appositive list could be defended) and no dash. Facts: khaddar ground cloth, untwisted silk floss (pat), darning from the back, as in standard craft descriptions.

band7.why: c468db1c shape: colon before a two-item list whose second item carries a which-clause with finite verbs; on target.

items.subtype: Restrictive appositive: descriptor and company name with no commas
items.passage: Swiss firms long dominated the manufacture of mechanical wristwatches. Their position began to erode in 1969, when Japanese ______ introduced the Astron, the first quartz wristwatch sold to consumers; inexpensive and remarkably accurate, quartz watches went on to capture much of the market.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Japanese watchmaker Seiko” works like a title and a name: “Japanese watchmaker” identifies which company is meant and is not set off as extra information, so no comma belongs between “watchmaker” and “Seiko.” No comma belongs after “Seiko” either, since that would separate the subject from its verb, “introduced.”

A.why_wrong: Commas around “Seiko” treat the name as removable extra information, but without an article “Japanese watchmaker” cannot stand alone as the subject; the name is essential.

B.why_wrong: The comma after “Seiko” separates the subject (“Japanese watchmaker Seiko”) from its verb (“introduced”).

D.why_wrong: A comma between “watchmaker” and “Seiko” splits the descriptor from the name it identifies; with no article before “Japanese watchmaker,” the name is restrictive and takes no comma.

items.notes: Subject: social science (business history, the quartz crisis). Band 6, on 4dcedc31 (“chemistry professor Yugang Sun and his colleagues”) and 80aa7690: the four comma patterns around descriptor + name, with the verb right after the name tempting B. Facts are the standard record (Seiko Astron, December 1969, first quartz wristwatch on sale; Swiss mechanical makers lost much of the market in the 1970s).

band7.why: 4dcedc31 menu (four comma patterns around descriptor + name, verb right after the name); on target.

items.subtype: Comma and coordinating conjunction between independent clauses; the second opens with a long introductory phrase
items.passage: Bucket orchids lure male euglossine bees with fragrant oils. A bee collecting these oils often slips into a pool of fluid in the flower’s bucket-shaped ______ while squeezing out through the sole exit, a narrow tunnel, it acquires a sticky packet of pollen on its back.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “A bee collecting these oils often slips into a pool of fluid in the flower’s bucket-shaped lip” and “while squeezing out through the sole exit, a narrow tunnel, it acquires a sticky packet of pollen on its back” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: When two long main clauses are joined with “and,” a comma is needed before the conjunction.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two main clauses; the long phrase “while squeezing out ... a narrow tunnel” makes the comma look natural, but “it acquires ...” is a second main clause.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “while squeezing out ...” attaches to the first clause, and the comma before “it acquires” then joins two main clauses: the clauses are not properly joined.

items.notes: Subject: science (orchid pollination). Planned band 7, written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/boundaries.md appendix). Band-6 setting from 59094d87: the second clause opens with a 10-word introductory phrase holding its own appositive, so the splice in B looks natural; menu of 59094d87 (and-without-comma, splice, fused). Facts: Coryanthes bees fall into the fluid-filled bucket and leave through a tunnel, picking up pollinia; no researchers named.

band7.why: S1_comma_conj has no band-7 official items, so it cannot be band 7; strong band 6 on 59094d87 with a 10-word intro phrase holding its own appositive in clause 2.

items.subtype: Closing dash of a pair that holds its own comma-set supplements
items.passage: In 1794, French engineer Claude Chappe’s optical telegraph began relaying dispatches between Paris and Lille. Each tower’s signaling apparatus—a long beam, called the regulator, with shorter arms, called indicators, pivoting at either ______ could be set in nearly a hundred distinct positions readable from the next tower.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “apparatus” opens a supplementary element that describes the apparatus (“a long beam, called the regulator, with shorter arms, called indicators, pivoting at either end”). A second dash after “end” closes that element, so the subject “Each tower’s signaling apparatus” connects to its verb, “could be set.”

A.why_wrong: The commas around “called the regulator” and “called indicators” are already paired; the element as a whole was opened with a dash, so it must be closed with a dash, not a comma.

C.why_wrong: Leaving out the closing dash runs the supplementary element into the main verb, so “Each tower’s signaling apparatus” never connects cleanly to “could be set.”

D.why_wrong: A semicolon cannot close a dash element, and it would separate the subject “Each tower’s signaling apparatus” from its verb “could be set.”

items.notes: Subject: history of technology (French Revolutionary era). Model 6e071432 (comma inside a dash pair) and 109d5bbb (dash element with an internal comma). Facts are the standard record: Chappe’s semaphore line Paris to Lille opened in 1794; each station had a regulator with two indicators, giving about 98 usable positions; no researchers named.
band7_moves: two levels of supplement: comma-set appositives (“called the regulator,” “called indicators”) inside the dash element, so the comma option looks like the natural closer (6e071432)
opening dash 16 words before the blank, outside a 6-word window
the element sits between subject and verb, so the partner is required for the sentence to parse

fixes: “a shorter arm, called an indicator, pivoting at either end” made plural (“shorter arms, called indicators”), since there is one at each end; boundary unchanged

band7.why: Two levels of supplement (comma-set “called” appositives inside the dash pair) as in 6e071432, opening dash 16 words before the blank, so a local reading picks the comma; 109d5bbb-type single slot.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a long subject and its verb
items.passage: Makonde artists of Tanzania and Mozambique work in African blackwood, an exceptionally dense hardwood. Inspired by spirits from Makonde folklore, the contorted, elongated figures that carvers in Tanzania began producing in the 1950s and ______ became known as shetani, after a Swahili word for a spirit.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The subject of the sentence is the long noun phrase “the contorted, elongated figures that carvers in Tanzania began producing in the 1950s and 1960s,” and its verb is “became.” No punctuation should separate a subject from its verb.

B.why_wrong: The long subject makes a pause feel natural, but a comma cannot separate the subject (“the contorted, elongated figures ... 1960s”) from its verb, “became.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon joins two main clauses; here it would cut the subject off from its verb, leaving neither side complete.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but the words before it are only the subject of the sentence.

items.notes: Subject: arts (East African sculpture). Band 6, on f868d438 and 2fd05c15: a 15-word subject with a restrictive relative clause and a date pair, after an introductory participial phrase, so a comma before the verb feels natural. Facts: shetani carving emerged among Makonde carvers in Tanzania from the late 1950s; the name is Swahili for a spirit or devil; no names.

band7.why: S4_subj_verb has no band-7 official items; strong band 6 with a 15-word subject carrying a restrictive clause and a date pair after an intro phrase.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around a long participial phrase between subject and verb
items.passage: Pansori, a Korean genre of sung storytelling, requires only two performers, a singer and a drummer. The drummer, seated on the floor beside the singer with a barrel-shaped drum known as a ______ maintains the rhythm and calls out exclamations of encouragement that spur the singer on.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “The drummer” opens a supplementary phrase (“seated on the floor beside the singer with a barrel-shaped drum known as a buk”). A comma after “buk” closes that phrase, so the subject “The drummer” connects to its verbs, “maintains” and “calls out.”

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the supplementary phrase opened by the comma after “The drummer” is never closed, and it runs straight into the verb “maintains.”

B.why_wrong: The phrase was opened with a comma, so it must be closed with a comma; a dash does not pair with a comma.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon would separate the subject “The drummer” from its verb “maintains,” leaving no complete clause on either side.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Korean music and storytelling). Planned band 7, written as a strong band 6 with band_target 6: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/boundaries.md appendix). The partner comma sits 14 words before the blank, and the phrase ends on a defining “known as a buk” that seems complete; the earlier appositive (“a singer and a drummer”) shows commas without a dash anywhere. Facts: pansori is performed by a singer and a drummer (gosu) on a buk, who calls out chuimsae; no names.

band7.why: S3_comma_pair has no band-7 official items; partner comma 14 words back and the phrase ends on a naming phrase that looks closed; band 6.

items.subtype: Comma and coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: In Japan, travelers are expected to bring back omiyage, gifts of food associated with the places they have visited. Such gifts are seldom intended for a single ______ they typically come as boxes of individually wrapped sweets that can be distributed to every member of an office or household.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Such gifts are seldom intended for a single recipient” and “they typically come as boxes of individually wrapped sweets ...” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “but” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: When “but” joins two main clauses this long, a comma is needed before it.

C.why_wrong: The comma before “but” is right, but no comma belongs after the conjunction; “but,” wrongly separates “but” from the clause it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: social science (Japanese gift customs). Medium on 2.12 (“skeptical, but historians”); the comma-after-conjunction decoy follows 2.17 (“paradox and,”) and 1.31 (“world, but,”). The relation (single recipient vs whole office) suits “but.” Facts general and well known; no names.

items.subtype: Period between independent clauses; the second opens with a short prepositional phrase
items.passage: In the early 1800s, Black Seminoles, many of whom had escaped slavery on plantations in neighboring Georgia, established settlements in Spanish Florida near Seminole villages. These allies fought beside the Seminole against the US ______ the conclusion of the Second Seminole War in 1842, most had been forcibly relocated to Indian Territory.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “These allies fought beside the Seminole against the US Army” is a complete sentence, and so is “By the conclusion of the Second Seminole War in 1842, most had been forcibly relocated to Indian Territory.” A period after “Army” correctly separates them.

B.why_wrong: A comma alone cannot join two main clauses; “most had been forcibly relocated ...” is a second main clause.

C.why_wrong: Without punctuation, “by the conclusion of the Second Seminole War” attaches to the first clause, and the comma after “1842” then joins two main clauses: a comma splice.

D.why_wrong: “And” cannot join these two long main clauses without a comma before it.

items.notes: Subject: history (Black Seminole communities in Florida). Medium: a 10-word prepositional opener (“By the conclusion of the Second Seminole War in 1842,”) as in 2.10 (“In 1420 CE,”) and 2.27 (“Prior to VisiCalc’s release,”). No semicolon or “, and” option. Facts: maroon towns allied with the Seminole in Spanish Florida, fighting in the Seminole Wars, removal of most to Indian Territory by the war’s end in 1842; no names.

fixes: capitalised “US Army” in the options and explanation (proper noun)

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing participial phrase
items.passage: The common potoo, a nocturnal bird of Central and South America, spends the daylight hours perched motionless on the stub of a broken branch, its eyes nearly closed and its bill pointed ______ its mottled gray-brown silhouette into a convincing imitation of weathered wood.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “The common potoo ... spends the daylight hours perched motionless on the stub of a broken branch, its eyes nearly closed and its bill pointed skyward” is a complete clause, and “transforming its mottled gray-brown silhouette into a convincing imitation of weathered wood” is a participial phrase that describes the effect of that posture. A comma correctly separates a main clause from a trailing phrase like this.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “transforming its mottled gray-brown silhouette ...” has no subject or main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “Transforming its mottled gray-brown silhouette into a convincing imitation of weathered wood” a sentence by itself, but it is only a phrase: a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, the phrase runs into the clause and seems to describe “skyward” rather than the bird’s whole posture; a trailing phrase like this is set off with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: science (bird camouflage). Medium on 2.4 (“CE, making”) and 2.26 (“fungi, producing”), with a different participle; the trailing phrase follows two absolute phrases, so the clause looks finished before it. Facts general (Nyctibius griseus roosts upright on branch stubs by day, eyes nearly closed, bill raised); no names.

items.subtype: Closing comma of a pair around a nonrestrictive where-clause
items.passage: Glagolitic, the oldest known Slavic alphabet, was created in the 860s by the missionary Constantine (later Saint Cyril), and although most Slavic communities eventually abandoned it, priests along Croatia’s Adriatic coast, where the script took on squarer, more angular ______ kept using it into the nineteenth century.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The comma after “coast” opens a nonessential clause (“where the script took on squarer, more angular forms”). A comma after “forms” closes it, so the subject “priests along Croatia’s Adriatic coast” connects to its verb, “kept.”

A.why_wrong: Without a closing comma, the where-clause opened after “coast” runs straight into the verb “kept.”

C.why_wrong: The clause was opened with a comma, so it must be closed with a comma, not a dash.

D.why_wrong: A semicolon would cut the subject “priests along Croatia’s Adriatic coast” off from its verb “kept.”

items.notes: Subject: language (Slavic writing systems). Medium on 2.6 (“according to Swentzell,”) and 2.14: the partner comma is 8 words before the blank, and the clause holds its own comma (“squarer, more angular”), which makes a bare “forms” look closed. Facts: Glagolitic devised by Constantine-Cyril in the 860s; an angular Croatian form persisted in Croatian church use into the 1800s; no researchers named.

items.subtype: Closing dash of a pair around an appositive between subject and verb
items.passage: Son jarocho, a musical tradition from the Mexican state of Veracruz, is performed at community celebrations called fandangos. There, the jarana—a small, eight-string guitar strummed in rapid, syncopated ______ is joined by a harp and by dancers whose footwork on a wooden platform adds a percussive layer.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: The dash after “jarana” opens a supplementary element that describes the instrument. A second dash after “patterns” closes it, so the subject “the jarana” connects to its verb, “is joined.”

A.why_wrong: The element was opened with a dash, so it must be closed with a dash; a comma does not pair with a dash.

B.why_wrong: Without a closing dash, the description of the jarana runs straight into the verb “is joined.”

C.why_wrong: A semicolon would cut the subject “the jarana” off from its verb “is joined,” leaving neither side a complete clause.

items.notes: Subject: arts (Mexican regional music). Medium on 2.13 (closing dash before “serves”): the dash element contains commas (“small, eight-string,” “rapid, syncopated”), so the comma option tempts; partner 8 words back. Facts general (jarana, harp, zapateado on a tarima at fandangos); no names.

fixes: removed an em dash from notes (quoted official text)

items.subtype: Colon after a complete clause before a single specified item
items.passage: Nitinol, a nickel-titanium alloy that metallurgist William Buehler began testing at the US Naval Ordnance Laboratory in 1959 as a potential material for missile nose cones, turned out to have an unexpected ______ ability to return to its original shape when heated after being bent or compressed.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Nitinol, a nickel-titanium alloy that ... William Buehler began testing ..., turned out to have an unexpected property” is a complete clause, and “the ability to return to its original shape ...” names that property. A colon correctly introduces an explanation after a complete clause.

A.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “the ability to return to its original shape ...” is a noun phrase with no main verb.

B.why_wrong: The period makes “The ability to return to its original shape when heated after being bent or compressed” a sentence by itself, but it has no main verb: a fragment.

D.why_wrong: With no punctuation, “property the ability ...” runs the explanation into the clause with nothing to introduce it.

items.notes: Subject: science and technology (shape-memory alloys). Medium on 2.15 (“new: sequencing”) menu, with a missing-mark option in place of 2.15’s misplaced colon; no comma option (a comma before an appositive could be defended) and no dash. Facts: Buehler at the Naval Ordnance Laboratory, 1959, nickel-titanium for missile nose cones; the name nitinol and its shape memory are the standard record.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a preposition and its object
items.passage: The elephantnose fish, found in murky rivers of West and Central Africa, hunts mostly at night. Its trunklike chin is covered with sensors that detect tiny distortions ______ the weak electric field the fish generates, allowing it to locate insect larvae buried in mud.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In the weak electric field” is a prepositional phrase that tells where the distortions occur. No punctuation belongs between the preposition “in” and its object, “the weak electric field.”

B.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate a preposition from its object.

C.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause; here it would split the preposition “in” from its object.

D.why_wrong: A dash has no role between a preposition and its object, and nothing in the sentence pairs with it.

items.notes: Subject: science (electric fish). Easy on 1.9 (“from”) and 1.23 (“to”): comma, colon and dash after a preposition. Facts general (Gnathonemus petersii senses its own weak field with electroreceptors on its chin appendage and finds larvae in mud); no names.

items.subtype: No punctuation between a verb and its objects
items.passage: Denmark’s first folk high school opened in 1844 in the town of Rødding. Shaped by the ideas of the Danish pastor and writer Nikolaj Grundtvig, such schools ______ adults short residential courses without exams or grades, emphasizing discussion, singing, and communal life over formal instruction.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: In “such schools offer adults short residential courses,” the verb “offer” is followed directly by its objects, “adults” and “short residential courses.” No punctuation belongs between a verb and its objects.

A.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, but “such schools offer” is not complete without its objects.

C.why_wrong: A comma cannot separate the verb “offer” from its objects.

D.why_wrong: A dash has no role between a verb and its objects, and nothing in the sentence pairs with it.

items.notes: Subject: social science (adult education in Denmark). Easy on 1.16 (“have unearthed”) and 1.15: verb and object, with colon, comma and dash decoys. Facts: Rødding, 1844; Grundtvig’s ideas; courses without exams; no researchers named.

items.subtype: Embedded question: statement word order and a period
items.passage: The Baikal seal is one of very few seals that live only in freshwater. Because its home, Siberia’s Lake Baikal, lies deep inside the Asian continent, researchers have long debated how ______ Many suspect that ancestral seals traveled upriver from the Arctic Ocean.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
options: did the seals reach the lake?
did the seals reach the lake.
items.explanation: “How the seals reached the lake” is an embedded question: it is the object of “debated,” not a question being asked directly. It therefore takes statement word order (“the seals reached”), and the sentence, a statement, ends with a period.

A.why_wrong: An embedded question does not use question word order (“did the seals reach”), and the sentence is a statement, so it cannot end with a question mark.

B.why_wrong: The period is correct, but question word order (“did the seals reach”) is wrong inside an embedded question.

C.why_wrong: The word order is correct, but the sentence is a statement about what researchers have debated, so it ends with a period, not a question mark.

items.notes: Subject: science (freshwater seals). Easy on 1.7 (“how much artificial sweetener most people prefer in a diet drink.”): the 2 x 2 grid of word order and end mark. Facts general (Pusa sibirica, only in Lake Baikal; ancestors thought to have arrived from the Arctic by river); no names.

items.subtype: Comma and coordinating conjunction between independent clauses
items.passage: Beginning in 1780, the Hudson’s Bay Company traded wool blankets to Indigenous trappers in exchange for beaver pelts. Each blanket had short black stripes woven into one ______ the number of these stripes, called points, indicated the blanket’s dimensions.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Each blanket had short black stripes woven into one edge” and “the number of these stripes, called points, indicated the blanket’s dimensions” are both main clauses. A comma followed by the coordinating conjunction “and” correctly joins them.

A.why_wrong: With no punctuation and no conjunction, the two main clauses run together.

B.why_wrong: When “and” joins two main clauses like these, a comma is needed before it.

D.why_wrong: The comma before “and” is right, but no comma belongs after it; “and,” wrongly separates the conjunction from the clause it introduces.

items.notes: Subject: history (North American fur trade). Easy on 1.27 and 1.31: fused, conjunction without comma, and comma after the conjunction (1.31 “world, but,”). Facts: Hudson’s Bay Company point blankets from about 1780, woven points indicating size; no names.

items.subtype: Comma after an introductory dependent clause
items.passage: At Makola Market in Accra, Ghana, traders who sell the same product, such as tomatoes or cloth, often choose a leader known as a market queen. Although these women hold no official government ______ settle disputes among traders and represent them in negotiations with city officials.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “Although these women hold no official government position” is a dependent clause that introduces the main clause “they settle disputes among traders and represent them in negotiations with city officials.” A comma correctly separates an introductory dependent clause from the main clause.

A.why_wrong: The period leaves “Although these women hold no official government position” as a sentence by itself, but it is a dependent clause: a fragment.

C.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but the clause beginning with “Although” is dependent.

D.why_wrong: A colon must follow a complete clause, and the “Although” clause is not one; what follows is not an explanation of it either.

items.notes: Subject: social science (market organization in West Africa). Easy on 1.8 (“Although ... asteroids, several”): the bank’s period, semicolon and colon decoys. Facts general (commodity groups at Makola choose market queens who settle disputes and deal with authorities); no names.

items.subtype: Comma before a trailing such as phrase
items.passage: The Book of Dede Korkut, a collection of twelve heroic tales of the Oghuz Turks, is known chiefly from two sixteenth-century manuscripts. In one tale, the young warrior Bamsı Beyrek wins the right to marry Banu Çiçek by beating her in several athletic ______ them horse racing, archery, and wrestling.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “In one tale, the young warrior Bamsı Beyrek wins the right to marry Banu Çiçek by beating her in several athletic contests” is a complete clause, and “among them horse racing, archery, and wrestling” is a supplementary phrase that names some of those contests. A comma correctly separates the clause from this trailing phrase.

B.why_wrong: A semicolon must join two main clauses, but “among them horse racing, archery, and wrestling” has no verb; it is only a phrase.

C.why_wrong: The period leaves “Among them horse racing, archery, and wrestling” as a sentence by itself, but it has no verb: a fragment.

D.why_wrong: Without a comma, “among them” runs straight into the clause, so “horse racing, archery, and wrestling” is left with no grammatical role; a supplementary phrase that names examples must be set off with a comma.

items.notes: Subject: literature (Turkic oral epic). Easy on 1.11 (“movie, such as”) and the trailing “among them” phrase of adf210e7: a trailing supplement after a complete clause, with semicolon, period and missing-comma decoys. Facts: twelve tales known chiefly from two sixteenth-century manuscripts (Dresden and Vatican; a third, partial manuscript surfaced in 2018, hence “chiefly”); Bamsı Beyrek’s contests with Banu Çiçek in riding, archery and wrestling; no researchers named.

fixes: “contests, such as” replaced by “contests, among them”: without a comma, “athletic contests such as horse racing, archery, and wrestling” reads as a restrictive “such as” and is defensible (CB itself writes “materials such as microphones” unpunctuated), so D was a second answer; “contests among them horse racing” has no such reading. Options, explanation, why_wrong B to D and notes rewritten

items.subtype: Restrictive that-clause: no comma before that
items.passage: In 2013, scientists at the Smithsonian Institution announced that the olinguito, a small, tree-dwelling mammal of the cloud forests of Colombia and Ecuador, was a previously unknown species. For decades, museum specimens of the animal had been mislabeled as olingos, close ______ are larger and live at lower elevations.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
items.explanation: “That are larger and live at lower elevations” is a restrictive clause: it belongs to “close relatives” and tells which relatives the specimens were confused with, so it is not an aside. A restrictive clause is not set off with punctuation, so no mark belongs between “relatives” and “that.”

A.why_wrong: A comma is not used before a restrictive clause beginning with “that.”

B.why_wrong: Without “that,” the verbs “are” and “live” have no subject linking them to “relatives,” so the sentence is ungrammatical.

C.why_wrong: A dash would separate the restrictive clause from the noun it defines, and nothing in the sentence pairs with it.

items.notes: Subject: science (mammal taxonomy). Easy on 1.29 (“company that”): comma before “that,” missing “that,” and a dash. Facts: olinguito announced as a new species by Smithsonian scientists in 2013; earlier specimens misidentified as olingos, which are larger and live lower; no names.

fixes: explanation reworded (it said the clause “identifies which close relatives olingos are”)
